title: Minimum spanning tree: edge-subset enumeration vs Kruskal (and Prim)
problem_statement: Given the complete undirected graph K_n on n >= 1 vertices with positive integer edge weights (a symmetric n x n weight matrix), compute the total weight of a minimum spanning tree. For n = 1 the answer is 0.

input.size_measure: m = n(n-1)/2 edge weights (Theta(n^2) input), integers below 10^9 in the harness, so arithmetic and comparisons are unit cost.

algorithms.name: enumeration of all (n-1)-edge subsets
algorithms.idea: Every spanning tree has exactly n-1 edges. Try each of the C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) subsets of n-1 edges; it is a spanning tree iff it connects all n vertices (one depth-first search). Keep the lightest.
algorithms.pseudocode: for each (n-1)-subset T of the edges: if T is connected: best = min(best, weight(T))
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1)) = 2^Theta(n log n) (C(m, n-1) subsets, Theta(n) each to build, search and weigh)
algorithms.correctness: Exhaustive. A graph with n vertices and n-1 edges is a tree iff it is connected, so the connected subsets are exactly the spanning trees.

algorithms.name: Kruskal with union-find
algorithms.idea: Sort the edges by weight and scan them, keeping each edge that joins two different components (tracked by union-find with union by size and path halving).
algorithms.time_complexity: O(m log m) = O(n^2 log n) on K_n (comparison sort of the m edges; the union-find work is O(m alpha(n)))
algorithms.correctness: Kruskal 1956. Cut property: the lightest edge crossing a cut that respects the current forest belongs to some minimum spanning tree containing that forest, so every edge kept is safe. Edges inside a component would close a cycle and are skipped.

algorithms.name: Prim, array version
algorithms.idea: Grow one tree from vertex 0. Keep for every outside vertex the cheapest edge to the tree; each round adds the closest outside vertex and updates the others by scanning its row.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on K_n (n-1 rounds, two Theta(n) scans each), linear in the input size
algorithms.correctness: Prim 1957. Each round adds the lightest edge crossing the cut (tree, rest), which is safe by the cut property.

relationship: Super-exponential -> polynomial: Theta(n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1)) = 2^Theta(n log n) vs O(n^2 log n) (Kruskal) and Theta(n^2) (Prim, linear in the input on dense graphs). The cut property makes greedy choices safe, so no search is needed. Even enumerating only the spanning trees would not help: K_n has n^(n-2) of them (Cayley's formula). On sparse graphs the line continues with Chazelle 2000 (O(m alpha(m, n)), deterministic) and Karger-Klein-Tarjan 1995 (expected O(m), randomized).

verification.method: V1: all three implementations agree for n = 1..7 (enumeration capped at n = 7, i.e. 54,264 subsets) on random weights in [1, 100] and, in some trials, in [1, 3] (many ties); Kruskal and Prim also agree at n = 20, 60 and 200. harness.check is independent of all three: Boruvka's algorithm with (w, u, v) tie-breaking, plus the bounds (sum of the n-1 lightest edges) <= answer <= (weight of the path 0-1-...-(n-1)). V2: runtimes fitted against n * C(n(n-1)/2, n-1), n^2 log n and n^2 on weights in [1, 10^9]. The enumeration can only be timed at n = 4..7 (n = 8 has 1,184,040 subsets, ~1.3 s per call); the n = 4 point is ~0.01 ms but is timed in loops, and the fit is stable. An earlier Kruskal version that sorted (w, u, v) tuples measured alpha ~1.19 because of cache effects once m exceeds ~10^5 edges; packing each edge into one integer key (same sort order) removed this.

caveats: On K_n Prim's Theta(n^2) array version is already optimal (linear in the input); Kruskal's sort makes it a log factor slower. The V2 fit for Kruskal cannot by itself resolve the log factor (log n varies only ~1.7x over the measured range), so it confirms ~n^2 growth up to logarithmic factors. Measured times include CPython memory effects that are outside the RAM model.
notes: The enumeration's count C(n(n-1)/2, n-1) grows like (e n / 2)^(n-1) up to polynomial factors; only n^(n-2) of these subsets are spanning trees (Cayley's formula).
